section.title: Graphing windows
section.p: A graph on a screen is not the graph itself.
It is a sampled picture of part of the graph, drawn in a chosen rectangle:
section.md: x_{\min}\le x\le x_{\max}, \qquad y_{\min}\le y\le y_{\max}.
section.p: Anything outside that rectangle is invisible. Anything between sampled points may be missed. A good graphing window reveals structure. A poor window hides it.

subsection.title: A window is a mathematical choice

figure.caption: The same function can tell a different visual story in different windows.

subsection.p: The function did not change. The picture changed.

note.title: Window habit
note.p: Before trusting a graph, change the window.
Try a smaller window, a larger window, and a window centered on important points: zeros, critical points, endpoints, and possible asymptotes.

subsection.title: A graph can hide a sharp feature
subsection.p: A graphing device samples finitely many points. If important behavior occurs between sampled points, the plotted graph may miss it.
For example,
oscillates rapidly. A coarse plot may connect sampled points in a way that looks much less oscillatory than the true function.

figure.caption: Sampling too few points can give a misleading picture of a rapidly changing function.

subsection.p: This matters in calculus because derivatives, roots, local extrema, asymptotes, and oscillations may all be small or narrow enough to be missed in a first plot.

subsection.title: A graphing checklist
subsection.p: When using a graphing tool, ask these questions.

row.cell: A plotted curve may hide holes or forbidden inputs.
Important behavior may lie outside the viewing rectangle.
Connecting across an asymptote can produce false lines.
Have I zoomed in near zeros and critical points?
Local behavior may be invisible at a large scale.
End behavior and global shape may be invisible at a small scale.
Factoring, derivatives, and limits reveal features a plot may miss.

note.title: Graphing principle
note.p: A graph is evidence. It is not a proof.
Use it to form guesses. Use algebra, calculus, and domain information to check them.
